before: Intrinsic sizes come from content. min-content seeks the narrowest size using allowed wrapping; max-content measures without those soft wraps. fit-content balances them against available space.

The HTML supplies the elements; CSS supplies their presentation. This small fixture uses horizontal writing and left-to-right direction. ```html
one two three
``` ```css .demo { writing-mode: horizontal-tb; direction: ltr; } .wrap { width: 100px; } .label { font: 16px/20px monospace; width: fit-content; } ```

width: fit-content uses a keyword, not a function. For this block it clamps available width between the min-content and max-content sizes. The normal spaces provide wrapping opportunities; the longest word limits how narrow it can become. font is fixed here only to make the example repeatable.
Use content-aware sizing for a short label. An unbreakable string may still overflow: fit-content is not a universal overflow fix. The separate fit-content(…) grid function is outside this lesson.
Fit the short label to its content within the 100px wrapper.
after: An intrinsic size is a size worked out from the content. `min-content` uses the narrowest width allowed by normal wrapping. `max-content` uses the width the content needs without wrapping at ordinary spaces.
Here, `fit-content` is a keyword, so it has no parentheses. The spaces between words are places where the text can wrap. The longest unbreakable word limits how narrow the label can become.
With `max-content`, the label would request enough width for all its words on one line. In this example, that would exceed the 100-pixel wrapper.

`fit-content` does not guarantee that all content will fit. One long word with no allowed break may still need more width than the wrapper has. This lesson uses the width keyword, not the separate grid function with the same name.
Keep the wrapper 100 pixels wide and set the label’s width to `fit-content`. Keep its words unchanged. Run the checks and inspect where the words wrap.

before.question: Why might fit-content still overflow with one very long unbreakable word?
choices: Its min-content width can exceed the available width
before.explanation: The content’s minimum can be larger than its container.

after.question: Why can fit-content still overflow when the label has one very long word?
choices: The word’s minimum width can be larger than the space available.
It removes spaces from the text.
after.explanation: A word that cannot break may need more room than the wrapper provides.
